\section{Background \& Related Work}\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Test-time compute scaling.}
Test-time compute scaling encompasses three families: (a) extended chain-of-thought reasoning \cite{muennighoff2025s1}, (b) repeated sampling with majority voting (self-consistency; \citealp{wang2023selfconsistency}) and its extensions to free-form text \cite{chen2024usc, thirukovalluru2024atomic, manakul2023selfcheckgpt}, and (c) best-of-$N$ selection via compute-optimal allocation \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
Reward-free selectors \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty, wang2025rankedvoting, oh2026latentsc} and adaptive gating variants \cite{aggarwal2023adaptive, wang2025make, feng2025optimal, kim2026reasc} reduce inference cost; \citet{chen2023twofailures} diagnose failure modes.
All target discrete-answer reasoning; structured prediction requires different aggregation mechanisms because degeneracy operates at the entity-set level.

\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
\citet{yao2026consistency} demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy for LLM-based NER/RE, establishing the QE value of consistency signals.
Our work addresses the complementary question: \textit{when and why} does this correlation translate into selection or construction gains?
We identify degeneracy and LP compression as two mechanisms that prevent strong QE from yielding selection improvements, providing a diagnostic characterization absent from their analysis.
CoCoA \cite{vashurin2025cocoa} fuses confidence with consistency; our supervised baseline confirms combination is not the bottleneck (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}).
Earlier work on confidence for structured prediction \cite{culotta2004confidence, mejer2010confidence, fomicheva2020unsupervised} establishes the paradigm we extend to set-valued outputs.
Ensemble approaches aggregate predictions from multiple models or prompts \cite{florian2003named, xiao2025el4ner}; \citet{xie2023zeroshot} propose two-stage entity voting for zero-shot NER, the closest prior work to our entity-level construction.
LLM-Blender \cite{jiang2023llmblender} fuses outputs from multiple LLMs via pairwise ranking, whereas our single-model stochastic sampling derives diversity from temperature rather than model heterogeneity.
Our entity-level construction aggregates across samples from a single fine-tuned model, without requiring model diversity or prompt engineering.
Our evaluation builds on generative IE \cite{zhou2024uniner, sainz2024gollie, li2023codeie, wadhwa2023revisiting, xie2024selfimproving} and constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided, dong2024xgrammar, park2024grammar, schall2025hidden}.
\citet{yun2025price} show structured formats induce diversity collapse; our LP compression (median range 0.041 nats; \S\ref{sec:discussion}) corroborates this for NER.

\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and MBR decoding.}
Surveys cover confidence estimation \cite{geng2024confidence}, uncertainty quantification \cite{xia2025survey, liu2025uqcc}, and abstention \cite{wen2025abstention}; semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic, farquhar2024detecting} and P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} provide model-internal alternatives.
Our selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, deguchi2024centroid}; unlike MT where MBR yields consistent gains \cite{freitag2022high} and code generation where execution-based MBR improves selection \cite{shi2022mbr}, instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom MBR needs even when utility is well-aligned ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
\citet{eikema2025structured} find MBR utilities degrade on structured outputs; our diagnosis is complementary: degeneracy, not utility misalignment, is the primary bottleneck.
Our QE results connect to selective prediction \cite{geifman2017selective, kuleshov2015calibrated, varshney2022investigating}: signals with AUROC up to 0.82 support abstention policies independent of sample selection.

\paragraph{Best-of-$N$ with learned verifiers.}
\citet{gao2023scaling} establish BoN scaling laws and \citet{chen2021evaluating} define the pass@$k$ metric for code generation; our unsupervised signals face a more fundamental limitation than reward overoptimization.
Trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, lightman2024verify, fernandes2022quality} and self-evaluation guided search \cite{xie2023selfevaluation} learn per-sample scoring.
CISC \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc} and Self-Certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty} derive per-sample confidence from hidden states rather than output statistics, but require architecture-specific access to intermediate representations; these hidden-state signals remain untested for structured prediction (\S Limitations).
Fine-tuning \cite{kirk2024understanding} and constrained decoding \cite{holtzman2020curious, vijayakumar2018diverse} both limit the diversity recoverable for selection.

\paragraph{Hallucination and factuality detection.}
SelfCheckGPT \cite{manakul2023selfcheckgpt} detects hallucinations by sampling multiple responses and measuring consistency, assuming sufficient cross-sample variation to distinguish factual from fabricated claims.
FActScore \cite{min2023factscore} decomposes generation into atomic facts verified against reference corpora; RefChecker \cite{hu2024refchecker} and SAFE \cite{wei2024long} extend this paradigm with reference-based and search-augmented verification.
Our work identifies a boundary condition for structured extraction: entity-level self-judgment yields AUROC${=}0.51$ (Appendix~\ref{app:self_verification}), indicating the model cannot distinguish correct from incorrect entities via re-prompting, though cross-sample frequency agreement (AUROC${=}0.87$) provides an effective alternative.
This suggests that consistency-based self-verification faces inherent limits when applied to set-valued structured outputs under constrained decoding.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We establish a capability ceiling for self-consistency in structured generation: seven independent methods for entity-level self-verification---spanning self-judgment, re-prompting, latent aggregation, sampling strategies, and trained verifiers---all fail to close the correlation-selection gap across three NER benchmarks and two model families.

Future work should investigate whether this ceiling persists at frontier scale and whether fine-tuning objectives that explicitly reward entity-level discrimination can break it.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Test-time compute scaling complements model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling}: repeated sampling with majority voting \cite{wang2023selfconsistency}, best-of-$N$ with learned verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, brown2024monkeys}, and extended chain-of-thought \cite{muennighoff2025s1} produce large gains on reasoning and code generation.
These successes share a structural prerequisite: the output space admits either exact equivalence classes (multiple-choice, numeric answers) or execution-based verification (code).
Named entity recognition (NER) breaks both assumptions.
The output is a set of typed entities; two samples from the same input routinely extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and no external oracle can adjudicate correctness at test time.
Without equivalence classes, majority voting reduces to heuristic frequency counting; without a verifier, best-of-$N$ requires a reliable proxy signal.
This structural mismatch raises a concrete question: can self-consistency signals that estimate quality well for reasoning tasks also \textit{select} better outputs or \textit{construct} better entity sets for structured generation?
We investigate this question for NER and validate the core findings on SQL parsing, treating NER as a representative instance of the broader set-valued generation problem.

The question has practical stakes beyond information extraction.
Hallucination detection methods such as SelfCheckGPT \cite{manakul2023selfcheckgpt} and FActScore \cite{min2023factscore} rely on cross-sample consistency to verify individual claims: if a model's outputs agree, the shared content is presumed factual.
This reasoning assumes entity-level self-verification works, that a model can reliably distinguish correct extractions from incorrect ones through self-judgment or re-prompting.
We show this assumption fails.
Three independent probes (entity self-judgment, multi-round re-prompting, latent-space aggregation) all yield chance-level or negative results for a fine-tuned 8B model on NER.
Recent work \cite{yao2026consistency} demonstrates that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy across benchmarks but does not diagnose \textit{when} or \textit{why} this correlation breaks down at the selection level.
Our diagnostic framework fills this gap: four failure modes (degeneracy, low agreement, false agreement, LP compression) explain why strong instance-level correlation coexists with negligible sample-level selection gain.

We call this disparity the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
Five quality estimation (QE) signals achieve rank correlations up to $\rho{=}0.45$ and AUROC up to 0.82 with oracle F1, yet no signal outperforms greedy decoding on SciERC ($p{>}0.05$ for all comparisons).
Only log-probability (LP) achieves a positive selection gain, and only on Few-NERD ($+1.39$\,pp; Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.019$, selection family $k{=}19$).
To test whether entity-level methods can close this gap, we evaluated seven approaches: entity self-judgment (ESJ), multi-round self-consistency (MRSC), latent-space aggregation (LSC), heterogeneous temperature sampling (Het-T), adaptive sampling budget (ASB), self-consistency distillation (SCD), and a supervised entity verifier.
All seven fail across three datasets and two model families.
ESJ achieves AUROC of 0.51 (indistinguishable from chance), while frequency-based agreement reaches 0.87.
MRSC produces $P(\text{yes})$ separation of 0.0006 between correct and incorrect entities.
The supervised verifier achieves entity-level AUC of 0.923 but translates to only $+0.30$\,pp F1, with negative cross-dataset transfer.
A hidden-state probe confirms that discriminative information exists in model representations but remains inaccessible through the prompt-based self-judgment interface.

These findings rest on controlled experiments across four NER benchmarks (SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}), two model families (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B), a 4B ablation, and sample sizes $N {\in} \{2, \ldots, 32\}$.
We extend to Qwen3-72B in the zero-shot regime to test whether the capability ceiling persists at larger scale.
Cross-task validation on Spider SQL parsing (GPT-5.5, $n{=}196$) confirms the diagnostic cascade: degeneracy reaches 87.2\%, and the F1 failure mode dominates.
Our prescriptive analysis identifies three escape routes that work precisely because they bypass entity-level self-verification: entity-level construction via majority vote ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD, Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.006$; $+1.02$\,pp on SciERC, $p{=}0.004$), cross-model ensemble ($+0.42$\,pp), and LP-based selection restricted to low-degeneracy regimes.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{Overview of the correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals estimate instance quality ($\rho$ up to 0.45; Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}). \textbf{Center}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates, so selection cannot outperform greedy. \textbf{Right}: entity-level construction via majority vote ($\theta{=}2/N$) bypasses the bottleneck ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Diagnostic framework.}
    A four-stage cascade (QE $\to$ degeneracy $\to$ agreement fidelity $\to$ LP compression) that identifies where and why self-consistency fails for structured generation, cross-task validated on NER and SQL parsing (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}, \S\ref{sec:discussion}).

    \item \textbf{Impossibility evidence.}
    Seven entity-level methods $\times$ three NER datasets $\times$ two model families all fail to close the correlation-selection gap, constituting systematic evidence for a capability ceiling in entity-level self-verification (\S\ref{sec:mechanistic}, \S\ref{sec:adaptive}).

    \item \textbf{Mechanistic explanation.}
    Hidden-state probing reveals that discriminative information exists in model representations (frequency agreement AUROC${=}0.87$) but the prompt-based self-judgment interface cannot access it (ESJ AUROC${=}0.51$), identifying an introspection limit rather than an information deficit (\S\ref{sec:mechanistic}).

    \item \textbf{Prescriptive escape routes.}
    Entity-level construction ($+1.02$\,--\,$1.40$\,pp), cross-model ensemble ($+0.42$\,pp), and regime-specific LP selection ($+1.39$\,pp on Few-NERD) succeed because they bypass entity-level self-verification.
    A degeneracy decomposition $\mathbb{E}[\Delta F_1] = (1{-}D) \cdot G_{\text{nd}} \cdot \alpha$ yields a critical threshold $\theta_{\text{crit}}{=}0.70$ above which self-consistency cannot yield meaningful improvement (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}, \S\ref{sec:theory}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Test-time compute scaling.}
Test-time compute scaling encompasses three families: (a) extended chain-of-thought reasoning \cite{muennighoff2025s1}, (b) repeated sampling with majority voting (self-consistency; \citealp{wang2023selfconsistency}) and its extensions to free-form text \cite{chen2024usc, thirukovalluru2024atomic, manakul2023selfcheckgpt}, and (c) best-of-$N$ selection via compute-optimal allocation \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
Reward-free selectors \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty, wang2025rankedvoting, oh2026latentsc} and adaptive gating variants \cite{aggarwal2023adaptive, wang2025make, feng2025optimal, kim2026reasc} reduce inference cost; \citet{chen2023twofailures} diagnose failure modes.
All target discrete-answer reasoning; structured prediction requires different aggregation mechanisms because degeneracy operates at the entity-set level.

\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
\citet{yao2026consistency} demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy for LLM-based NER/RE, establishing the QE value of consistency signals.
Our work addresses the complementary question: \textit{when and why} does this correlation translate into selection or construction gains?
We identify degeneracy and LP compression as two mechanisms that prevent strong QE from yielding selection improvements, providing a diagnostic characterization absent from their analysis.
CoCoA \cite{vashurin2025cocoa} fuses confidence with consistency; our supervised baseline confirms combination is not the bottleneck (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}).
Earlier work on confidence for structured prediction \cite{culotta2004confidence, mejer2010confidence, fomicheva2020unsupervised} establishes the paradigm we extend to set-valued outputs.
Ensemble approaches aggregate predictions from multiple models or prompts \cite{florian2003named, xiao2025el4ner}; \citet{xie2023zeroshot} propose two-stage entity voting for zero-shot NER, the closest prior work to our entity-level construction.
LLM-Blender \cite{jiang2023llmblender} fuses outputs from multiple LLMs via pairwise ranking, whereas our single-model stochastic sampling derives diversity from temperature rather than model heterogeneity.
Our entity-level construction aggregates across samples from a single fine-tuned model, without requiring model diversity or prompt engineering.
Our evaluation builds on generative IE \cite{zhou2024uniner, sainz2024gollie, li2023codeie, wadhwa2023revisiting, xie2024selfimproving} and constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided, dong2024xgrammar, park2024grammar, schall2025hidden}.
\citet{yun2025price} show structured formats induce diversity collapse; our LP compression (median range 0.041 nats; \S\ref{sec:discussion}) corroborates this for NER.

\paragraph{LLM self-evaluation and introspection.}
P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} elicits the model's own correctness probability; Self-Certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty} derives confidence from hidden-state consistency; verbalized confidence \cite{xiong2024verbalized} prompts the model to estimate uncertainty in natural language.
These methods assume models possess reliable self-knowledge about their outputs.
Our entity self-judgment probe (AUROC${=}0.51$; \S\ref{sec:mechanistic}) provides direct evidence that this assumption fails for structured extraction: the model cannot distinguish correct from incorrect entities via re-prompting, even when the same information is recoverable from output distributions (frequency agreement AUROC${=}0.87$).
This identifies a gap between distributional and introspective self-knowledge specific to set-valued outputs.

\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and MBR decoding.}
Surveys cover confidence estimation \cite{geng2024confidence}, uncertainty quantification \cite{xia2025survey, liu2025uqcc}, and abstention \cite{wen2025abstention}; semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic, farquhar2024detecting} and P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} provide model-internal alternatives.
Our selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, deguchi2024centroid}; unlike MT where MBR yields consistent gains \cite{freitag2022high} and code generation where execution-based MBR improves selection \cite{shi2022mbr}, instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom MBR needs even when utility is well-aligned ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
\citet{eikema2025structured} find MBR utilities degrade on structured outputs; our diagnosis is complementary: degeneracy, not utility misalignment, is the primary bottleneck.
Our QE results connect to selective prediction \cite{geifman2017selective, kuleshov2015calibrated, varshney2022investigating}: signals with AUROC up to 0.82 support abstention policies independent of sample selection.

\paragraph{Best-of-$N$ with learned verifiers.}
\citet{gao2023scaling} establish BoN scaling laws and \citet{chen2021evaluating} define the pass@$k$ metric for code generation; our unsupervised signals face a more fundamental limitation than reward overoptimization.
Trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, lightman2024verify, fernandes2022quality} and self-evaluation guided search \cite{xie2023selfevaluation} learn per-sample scoring.
CISC \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc} and Self-Certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty} derive per-sample confidence from hidden states rather than output statistics, but require architecture-specific access to intermediate representations; these hidden-state signals remain untested for structured prediction (\S Limitations).
Fine-tuning \cite{kirk2024understanding} and constrained decoding \cite{holtzman2020curious, vijayakumar2018diverse} both limit the diversity recoverable for selection.

\paragraph{Hallucination and factuality detection.}
SelfCheckGPT \cite{manakul2023selfcheckgpt} detects hallucinations by sampling multiple responses and measuring consistency, assuming sufficient cross-sample variation to distinguish factual from fabricated claims.
FActScore \cite{min2023factscore} decomposes generation into atomic facts verified against reference corpora; RefChecker \cite{hu2024refchecker} and SAFE \cite{wei2024long} extend this paradigm with reference-based and search-augmented verification.
Our work identifies a boundary condition for structured extraction: entity-level self-judgment yields AUROC${=}0.51$ (Appendix~\ref{app:self_verification}), indicating the model cannot distinguish correct from incorrect entities via re-prompting, though cross-sample frequency agreement (AUROC${=}0.87$) provides an effective alternative.
This suggests that consistency-based self-verification faces inherent limits when applied to set-valued structured outputs under constrained decoding.

\section{Why Self-Verification Fails}\label{sec:mechanistic}

The diagnostic cascade (\S\ref{sec:method}) identifies \textit{where} self-consistency fails; this section probes \textit{why} by testing whether models can self-verify at the entity level.
We evaluate three independent probes on Qwen2.5-7B fine-tuned on Few-NERD ($N{=}8$, seed 42; full results in Appendix~\ref{app:self_verification}).

\paragraph{Entity Self-Judgment (ESJ).}
For each extracted entity, we prompt the generating model: ``Is [\textit{entity}] a [\textit{type}] entity in this sentence?''
Entity-level AUROC is $0.512$---indistinguishable from chance---with P(yes$|$correct)${=}0.500$ and P(yes$|$incorrect)${=}0.500$.
ESJ-weighted construction degrades F1 to $0.711$ (vs.\ greedy $0.794$).

\paragraph{Multi-Round Self-Consistency (MRSC).}
Re-prompting on disputed entities (agreement ${<}0.6$) with focused verification yields P(yes) separation of $0.0006$ between gold and non-gold entities ($0.5003$ vs.\ $0.4997$).
MRSC best F1 ($0.763$) falls below greedy.

\paragraph{Latent Self-Consistency (LSC).}
Mean-pooled final-layer hidden states ($d{=}3584$) provide per-sample latent representations.
Centroid selection ($0.759$) underperforms greedy ($0.779$); latent entity confidence ($0.839$) marginally outperforms majority vote ($0.837$) without closing the oracle gap ($0.867$).

\paragraph{The asymmetry.}
Cross-sample frequency agreement achieves entity-level AUROC${=}0.868$---the only effective entity-level signal---while all three self-verification probes fail.
Models encode entity-level quality in output \textit{distributions} (which entities recur across samples) rather than in per-sample self-evaluation capacity (whether the model can judge its own extractions).
This asymmetry---strong distributional signal, absent introspective signal---explains why entity-level construction succeeds (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}) while selection based on self-judgment does not.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

NER exhibits oracle scaling comparable to reasoning ($c{\approx}0.5$; \S\ref{sec:scaling}), but aggregation cannot close the gap: degeneracy (17.8--67.9\%), limited headroom, and LP-quality alignment ($\rho$ 0.043--0.667) constrain it.
Temperature disentangles these at $T{=}1.2$ (degeneracy 14.9\%, LP $\rho{=}0.225$; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}).

\paragraph{From diagnosis to practice.}\label{sec:selection_method}
Entity-level construction bypasses both failure mechanisms, with gains positive when degeneracy ${<}22$\% and absent when ${>}31$\% (all $p{<}0.01$; Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}). Under 72B few-shot, construction fails yet QE remains effective (SJ $\rho$ 0.29--0.44; Appendix~\ref{app:fs_error}).
Alternative strategies (DALS, MBR, DGS) and supervised mixtures fail to beat greedy (Appendix~\ref{app:dals}, \ref{app:supervised_combination}, \ref{app:when_selection_works}).

\paragraph{LP compression and calibration.}
LP compression connects to broader calibration challenges in fine-tuned LLMs \cite{kadavath2022language, xiong2024verbalized}: teacher-forcing training and constrained decoding compress the LP dynamic range, leaving within-instance variation insufficient for sample discrimination (median LP range 0.041 nats on SciERC; Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}).
\citet{yun2025price} observe similar diversity collapse under structured output formats.
Potential remedies---per-token LP variance, calibration-aware scoring, or temperature-adjusted LP---remain untested for entity-level ranking.
Two per-sample alternatives could bypass the LP compression bottleneck: Self-Certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty} derives confidence from consistency of token-level self-evaluation, while P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} elicits the model's own correctness probability.
Both produce per-sample scores without relying on sequence-level log-probabilities; whether they suffer similar compression under fine-tuning with constrained decoding is an open question.
